title: A read has not reserved the unit
prompt: A and B each want the last unit. After both READs under the conditional strategy, predict their observations, shared remaining units and accepted allocations. Has either reservation acquired the unit?
lookFor: A and B both have READ_OBSERVED with observedRemaining 1. Shared remaining is 1, allocated is 0, and the allocation list is empty.
explanation: Java records B's observation of 1 beside A's earlier observation of 1. Both actor statuses are READ_OBSERVED, while remaining stock stays 1, allocated units stay 0 and accounted units are 1. All three invariant flags are true. Neither read appended an allocation. Under this conditional strategy the observations are previews: each later attempt will check current stock. This snapshot says nothing yet about either acceptance decision.

tradeoff.prompt: A teammate wants to tell the caller that seeing available stock guarantees the reservation. Which response fits this evidence?

options.label: Treat the read as a preview and confirm at the acceptance boundary
options.feedback: The selected read has no allocation. The service needs an explicit check-and-change boundary before promising a reservation; the protected strategy checks current stock there.

options.label: Treat the available-stock response as a confirmed reservation
options.feedback: A's observation is 1, but Java still reports zero allocated units and no allocation records. Another reservation can act before A attempts.

title: The first acceptance looks consistent
prompt: Both reservations have observed 1. Inspect A's stale attempt before B attempts: predict the checked value, remaining units, allocated units and B's saved observation. Can this step certify the whole schedule?
lookFor: A checks SNAPSHOT 1, accepts quantity 1 and assigns remaining 0. Allocated units are 1; B remains READ_OBSERVED with its saved 1. All three checks still hold here.
explanation: A uses its saved observation: 1 minus quantity 1 assigns remaining 0 and appends A's allocation. Java reports allocated 1 and accounted 1, with nonnegative stock, capacity and conservation all preserved at this selected step. B still retains observedRemaining 1 and has not attempted. A consistent prefix cannot certify that B's later stale assignment preserves the rule. Acceptance is local model state, not a durable commit.

tradeoff.prompt: The dashboard is green immediately after A accepts. What should the reviewer examine before trusting the stale algorithm?

options.label: Inspect B's later attempt and its decision source
options.feedback: B's saved 1 survives A's change to current 0. The later step is the counterexample, so a passing selected prefix does not prove safety for the full schedule.

options.label: Approve the algorithm because this selected step passed
options.feedback: The three Java flags describe the selected prefix. They do not predict or approve the unobserved later step, where B can allocate from its stale value.

title: Two acceptances spend one observed unit
prompt: A has already allocated the last unit. B still remembers 1. Predict B's checked value, assignment, total allocated units and each invariant flag under the stale strategy.
lookFor: B checks SNAPSHOT 1 and is accepted. Its assignment leaves remaining 0 again; allocated becomes 2. Nonnegative stock stays true, but capacity and conservation are false.
explanation: B checks saved 1 against quantity 1 and writes 1 minus 1 equals 0, replacing the shared value that was already 0. Java appends B's allocation beside A's, so allocated units become 2 and accounted units become 0 plus 2 equals 2, although initial stock was 1. Remaining stock is nonnegative; allocatedWithinCapacity and unitsConserved are false. The whole-schedule firstViolationStepId is attempt-b. This is stale assignment, not decrementing current stock to minus one.

tradeoff.prompt: A teammate proposes adding only a check that remaining stock never goes below zero. What does this counterexample require instead?

options.label: Protect the current condition, stock change and allocation together
options.feedback: The counter stays nonnegative while two units are allocated from one. The proposed boundary must protect the relationship between stock and recorded allocations, not only the sign of a counter.

options.label: Use nonnegative remaining stock as the complete safety test
options.feedback: Java reports remaining 0 with nonnegative=true in this failing state. That single check misses both capacity and conservation breaches.

title: Name what acceptance protects together
prompt: Keep the shared-read schedule but choose the conditional strategy. At A's attempt, predict the decision source and shared-state changes. Which three parts form the protected action?
lookFor: A checks CURRENT 1 for quantity 1, leaves remaining 0 and appends A's allocation. Allocated is 1, accounted is 1, and every invariant flag is true.
explanation: A's attempt checks current shared stock 1, subtracts quantity 1 and appends its allocation in one indivisible modeled transition. Java reports remaining 0, allocated 1 and accounted 1, with all three flags preserved. The protected scope includes the current condition, stock mutation and allocation record. B's earlier observed value remains 1; this snapshot does not claim B has already been rejected. A's acceptance supplies no crash, durability, rollback or external-effect guarantee.

tradeoff.prompt: The production service atomically changes its counter, then independently records the reservation. What boundary would you review?

options.label: Verify coordination of the current check, counter and reservation record
options.feedback: The model protects all three inside one action. A separate record write falls outside a counter-only boundary; the real transaction and failure behavior need their own evidence.

options.label: Assume a counter-only atomic update establishes the full model guarantee
options.feedback: The invariant connects remaining stock with allocation records. Atomicity of one counter alone does not establish that the separate record stays coordinated or survives failure consistently.

title: The saved preview does not decide B's attempt
prompt: B earlier observed 1, but A has now allocated the unit. Predict B's checked value, status, retained observation and rejection reason. Does rejecting B change stock or the allocation list?
lookFor: B retains observedRemaining 1 but checks CURRENT 0, becomes REJECTED and reports INSUFFICIENT_STOCK. Remaining stays 0 and allocated stays 1, with only A's allocation.
explanation: The conditional decision uses current 0, not B's saved preview 1. Quantity 1 no longer fits, so Java reports RESERVATION_REJECTED with INSUFFICIENT_STOCK. B's status becomes REJECTED while its observation remains 1. Remaining stock stays 0, the allocation list still contains only A, allocated units are 1, and all three flags remain true. Rejection changes actor state; it does not append an allocation. The valid schedule still completes successfully as a model run.

tradeoff.prompt: A caller previously saw available stock but receives this rejection. How should the service describe the outcome?

options.label: Explain that another reservation won before the current-state check
options.feedback: A preview can become stale. The authoritative acceptance boundary now sees no available unit, so a readable insufficient-stock business outcome is consistent with the protected rule.

options.label: Promise that retrying the same quantity must eventually succeed
options.feedback: The model supplies neither replenishment nor retries, fairness or idempotency. Repeating a request does not establish that another unit exists or that an uncertain earlier effect is deduplicated.

title: One serial test can hide the race
prompt: Move B's read after A's attempt: READ A, ATTEMPT A, READ B, ATTEMPT B. Under the stale strategy, predict B's observation and outcome. What does this passing run fail to prove?
lookFor: B observes 0 after A accepts, then checks SNAPSHOT 0 and rejects. Remaining 0 plus allocated 1 accounts for initial 1, so all three flags are true for this order.
explanation: In this serial schedule A accepts before B reads. B therefore saves 0 and later checks that saved 0 against quantity 1, producing INSUFFICIENT_STOCK. Java reports one allocation, remaining 0, allocated 1 and accounted 1, with all checks preserved. The stale algorithm did not gain a current-state guarantee; this favorable input order removed the conflicting shared reads. Returning to READ A, READ B, ATTEMPT A, ATTEMPT B exposes its breach.

tradeoff.prompt: A test suite contains only this successful serial order. What additional test best challenges the claimed reservation guarantee?

options.label: Test a legal order where both read before either attempt
options.feedback: The shared-read fixture lets both actors save 1, exposing the decision-source difference. Legal interleavings test the mechanism; their counts are not production failure probabilities.

options.label: Repeat the same serial schedule and call that concurrent coverage
options.feedback: Repeating a deterministic input reproduces the same favorable order. It does not evaluate the competing stale observations that caused the counterexample.

title: Capacity can pass while units stop adding up
prompt: Start with two units; A and B each request one and both read 2. Under stale assignment, predict the final remaining, allocated and accounted units. Which check fails even if allocated units fit capacity?
lookFor: B checks SNAPSHOT 2 and writes remaining 1 again. Allocated is 2 and accounted is 3. Nonnegative stock and capacity are true, but conservation is false.
explanation: A assigns 2 minus 1 equals 1 and allocates one unit. B repeats that saved-value assignment, leaving remaining 1 while the allocation list grows to two units. Java reports accountedUnits 3 against initial stock 2. Two allocated units fit initial capacity, and remaining is nonnegative, but remaining plus allocated does not equal initial stock. Thus only unitsConserved is false at attempt-b. The broken counter/allocation relationship can exist without allocating above capacity.

tradeoff.prompt: Operations reports no capacity breach in this run. What evidence should the teammate still reconcile?

options.label: Check the stock and allocation relationship as a separate rule
options.feedback: Java's accounted 3 exceeds initial 2 even though allocated 2 fits capacity 2. Reconciliation must address that relationship; capacity and conservation are distinct checks.

options.label: Conclude that passing capacity proves all reservation data consistent
options.feedback: This selected outcome passes capacity while failing conservation. A green capacity flag does not replace the other Java-reported invariants.

title: Zero stock produces valid rejected work
prompt: Initial stock is zero and both reservations request one. At A's first attempt, predict its checked value, both actor statuses, allocation records and invariant flags. Is insufficient stock an invalid schedule or a valid business result?
lookFor: Both actors observed 0. A checks SNAPSHOT 0, becomes REJECTED and reports INSUFFICIENT_STOCK; B is still READ_OBSERVED. Remaining, allocated and accounted units are 0; allocations are empty and all flags are true.
explanation: Zero initial stock is valid model input. Both reads save 0. A then checks saved 0 against quantity 1 and rejects without changing shared stock or appending an allocation. At this selected step A is REJECTED, while B is still READ_OBSERVED and has not attempted; both retain observations 0. Java reports remaining 0, allocated 0, accounted 0 and all three invariant flags true. This is a valid insufficient-stock business decision. Attempt-before-read validation or an unavailable API supplies different evidence. B's later rejection is outside this selected snapshot.

tradeoff.prompt: The API evaluates this valid empty-stock workload. How should the app communicate the result and next action?

options.label: Show the rejected business decisions and let the learner change the workload
options.feedback: Java completed the legal schedule and preserved the invariants. Keep the explicit rejection evidence visible; zero stock is a meaningful experiment, not missing data.

options.label: Replace the result with a generic execution failure
options.feedback: The schedule is valid and has returned authoritative decisions. Calling every business rejection a server failure hides the reason and confuses it with an unavailable model.

title: An abort label cannot undo a published write
prompt: One unit is available. A publishes its stock decrement, then aborts before recording an allocation. Predict the remaining stock, visible allocations, revision and two checks: conservation and absence of aborted effects.
lookFor: A is ABORTED with USER_ABORT, but its appliedStockUnits is 1. Published remaining is 0, allocated is 0 and revision is 1. Conservation and abortedEffectsAbsent are both false.
explanation: At abort-a, Java clears no published stock: the split mode has no common undo boundary. A retains baseRemaining 1 and baseRevision 0 as history, has appliedStockUnits 1 and has no private workspace. The published allocation list is empty, so accounted units are 0 against initial 1. Nonnegative stock and capacity pass; conservation and absence of aborted effects fail. The first whole-history violation was decrement-a, before this abort. Calling a transaction ABORTED does not itself reverse its earlier writes.

tradeoff.prompt: A teammate adds an ABORTED status after two independent writes fail partway through. What evidence is needed before claiming the operation left no effects?

options.label: Inspect the actual related writes and their failure boundary
options.feedback: The returned actor is aborted while published stock is still reduced. Verify what is coordinated or undone at the real storage boundary, including each related record.

options.label: Treat the terminal status as proof that nothing changed
options.feedback: Java explicitly reports an aborted actor with a visible stock effect. A status value is evidence about control flow, not automatic undo of earlier independent writes.

title: Discard a proposal without changing shared stock
prompt: Run the same BEGIN, decrement, ABORT program with private preparation. Predict the published state after abort and what remains of A's private work and captured base.
lookFor: Published remaining stays 1, allocated stays 0 and revision stays 0. A is ABORTED with USER_ABORT; pending stock is 0, workingRemaining and pendingAllocation are absent, while baseRemaining 1 and baseRevision 0 remain.
explanation: The decrement prepared workingRemaining 0 privately; it never published stock. At abort-a, Java discards A's workspace and reports appliedStockUnits 0 and pendingStockUnits 0. Captured base 1 at revision 0 remains as history, not pending work. Published remaining 1 plus allocated 0 still accounts for the initial unit. All four checks and the whole-history invariant status are preserved. This is discard of unpublished local work, not a demonstration of real database rollback or crash recovery.

tradeoff.prompt: How would you explain the unchanged public state to a teammate?

options.label: The private proposal was discarded before any publication
options.feedback: The published revision never advanced. There was no public stock decrement to reverse in this mode; the retained base only explains where the proposal began.

options.label: A public decrement was applied and later reversed
options.feedback: Java never published the staged decrement. Describing an undo would teach a storage operation that this model does not perform.

title: A private zero is a proposal, not visible stock
prompt: A began with one unit at revision 0 and privately decrements one. Before RECORD or COMMIT, predict shared stock, A's working stock, pending stock and allocation records.
lookFor: Java checks WORKING_COPY 1. Shared remaining is 1 with revision 0 and no allocation. A is OPEN with workingRemaining 0 and pendingStockUnits 1, but no pending allocation yet.
explanation: At decrement-a, Java reports STOCK_STAGED: A's captured base remains 1 at revision 0, workingRemaining is the known value 0, and pendingStockUnits is 1. appliedStockUnits is 0 and pendingAllocation is absent. Published remaining 1 and allocated 0 preserve all four checks. The later full run commits one transaction and finishes with remaining 0 and allocated 1; those whole-run facts must not be presented as already visible at this selected step.

tradeoff.prompt: A reviewer sees workingRemaining 0 and says other callers must now see stock 0. What should you clarify?

options.label: Separate A's private proposal from published inventory
options.feedback: The selected Java state has private workingRemaining 0 beside public remainingUnits 1. Only a successful publication boundary makes the prepared pair visible.

options.label: Use the private value as the current public stock
options.feedback: The public value is still 1 at revision 0. Substituting the private number would invent an earlier visible write and hide the purpose of staging.

title: Publish both related changes at one boundary
prompt: A has privately prepared the stock decrement and allocation from revision 0. Predict the expected and actual revision checked by COMMIT, the published pair, and what happens to private work.
lookFor: COMMIT checks expected revision 0 against actual revision 0. Published remaining becomes 0 and allocated becomes 1 together, at revision 1. A is COMMITTED and its workspace is cleared.
explanation: Java publishes A's prepared stock and allocation in one modeled transition after the revisions match. The allocation was prepared at record-a and published at commit-a. A retains baseRemaining 1 and baseRevision 0, records appliedStockUnits 1, and clears workingRemaining, pendingAllocation and pendingStockUnits. All four checks are true, accounted units are 1, and no earlier public prefix violated them. COMMITTED names this local publication; it does not establish durability, database isolation or an external side effect.

tradeoff.prompt: A service must change a quota and insert its usage record. What should the engineer establish before promising this example's guarantee?

options.label: Identify the real boundary that coordinates both changes and handles failure
options.feedback: The model includes both stock and allocation in one publication. A real design needs evidence for its own storage transaction and failure behavior; a method name alone does not establish that boundary.

options.label: Rename the last method commit and assume durable atomic behavior
options.feedback: A label cannot extend the actual protected scope. This Java analysis deliberately omits disks, crashes, recovery and external effects.

title: A repaired final state keeps its earlier breach
prompt: With split writes, A decrements stock, records its allocation and finishes COMMITTED. Predict the final four flags and revision. Does that green final state erase the earlier stock-only prefix?
lookFor: Final remaining is 0, allocated is 1 and revision is 2; all four final flags are true. Whole-history invariantStatus is VIOLATED, with firstViolationStepId decrement-a.
explanation: The split decrement immediately made public remaining 0 while no allocation existed, breaking conservation at decrement-a. RECORD later published the row and repaired the arithmetic; COMMIT changes status only, leaving revision 2. The row was both prepared and published at record-a. At the selected commit, A is COMMITTED with appliedStockUnits 1, no private workspace and no failure reason. All final checks pass, but Java still reports the earlier violated prefix. Inspecting final values alone cannot establish that every public intermediate state was consistent.

tradeoff.prompt: A final reconciliation shows correct totals. What additional question follows from this run?

options.label: Ask whether a consumer could have observed an inconsistent intermediate state
options.feedback: The whole-history summary preserves the first public breach even after totals recover. Review the actual visibility boundary and what intermediate readers or failures can expose.

options.label: Declare every intermediate state safe because the final totals match
options.feedback: The stock-only prefix already failed conservation. Later repair changes final state; it does not remove that earlier evidence.

title: Conserved totals can still contain aborted effects
prompt: A has independently published both its stock decrement and allocation, then aborts. Predict whether the allocation still counts and which final check distinguishes this case from a clean abort.
lookFor: The published row remains: remaining 0 plus allocated 1 still accounts for initial 1 at revision 2. Conservation is true, but abortedEffectsAbsent is false and one aborted transaction has visible effects.
explanation: At abort-a, A becomes ABORTED with USER_ABORT but retains appliedStockUnits 1. Its allocation, prepared and published at record-a, stays in the public list and counts toward allocatedUnits 1. Nonnegative stock, capacity and conservation are true; absence of aborted effects is false. Private work is absent and base history remains 1 at revision 0. The earlier stock-only prefix also violated conservation. Excluding an aborted actor's visible row from the display would conceal the effect instead of undoing it.

tradeoff.prompt: A dashboard proposes hiding allocation rows whose actor status is ABORTED. What is the more useful engineering response?

options.label: Keep visible effects counted and investigate the actual failure boundary
options.feedback: The record still exists and the stock effect remains. Correct accounting must reflect the evidence, then establish how the real system prevents or handles those effects.

options.label: Hide the row and treat the abort as effect free
options.feedback: Filtering a row out of a report does not remove its published stock or allocation effect. It would also misrepresent the Java state.

title: Blocked work is an explicit business outcome
prompt: Stock begins at zero. A's stock command was rejected, and the legal program now reaches RECORD_ALLOCATION. Predict A's phase, pending values, public records and the outcome reason before its terminal command.
lookFor: RECORD reports WORK_SKIPPED with INSUFFICIENT_STOCK. A is still BLOCKED with workingRemaining 0, pendingStockUnits 0 and no pending allocation. Public remaining, allocated and revision are all 0; all four checks pass.
explanation: The earlier decrement checked WORKING_COPY 0 and blocked A. The selected record-a step explicitly skips the allocation rather than inventing success or dropping the step. A retains baseRemaining 0 and baseRevision 0, has no applied stock, and remains BLOCKED with INSUFFICIENT_STOCK. Its workingRemaining is the known value 0, not absent workspace. The later COMMIT becomes TRANSACTION_ABORTED with the same reason and clears that workspace. The valid model run completes; a business abort is different from invalid input or an unavailable API.

tradeoff.prompt: How should an app present this returned analysis?

options.label: Show the explicit skipped work and let the learner change the workload
options.feedback: The legal program was evaluated and no allocation was published. Its business reason is useful evidence and must remain distinct from network or validation errors.

options.label: Replace the analysis with a generic server failure
options.feedback: No execution failure occurred. A generic error would hide the modeled stock rejection, skipped step and later abort.

title: Enough stock does not make a stale base current
prompt: A and B each prepared one unit from stock 3 at revision 0. A has published first, leaving stock 2 at revision 1. Predict B's revision check, result and private-work cleanup. Does sufficient current stock guarantee its commit?
lookFor: B expects revision 0 but sees 1 and aborts with REVISION_CONFLICT. Published remaining stays 2 and allocated stays 1, with only A's allocation. B's private workspace is cleared; all four checks remain true.
explanation: The coarse revision covers visible inventory and allocation mutations. A's publication changed it from 0 to 1, so B's captured base is no longer current even though B's quantity 1 would fit public stock 2. At commit-b, B is ABORTED with appliedStockUnits 0, pendingStockUnits 0 and absent workingRemaining and pendingAllocation. B retains baseRemaining 3 and baseRevision 0 as history. A remains COMMITTED; its allocation was prepared at record-a and published at commit-a. Java reports one commit, one conflicted abort, no aborted transaction with effects and no violated prefix. This conservative conflict rule models neither automatic retry nor a SQL isolation level.

tradeoff.prompt: The product wants B to try again when capacity still exists. What additional design work is needed?

options.label: Design a fresh attempt with explicit retry and duplicate-effect rules
options.feedback: The model only discards this stale proposal. A real retry needs a fresh read plus bounded policy and handling of uncertain prior effects; none follows automatically from spare stock.

options.label: Ignore the revision mismatch because quantity 1 fits stock 2
options.feedback: That replaces the modeled validation rule without proving that its prepared stock and allocation remain valid. The returned abort preserves another transaction's published data.
